slides: Okay, a closer look at one of the points of view: rights. It's on our list, and it deserves its own lesson.
Which rights are there? What does the state owe us? And how do we turn a right into an argument?
So, rights. One of our points of view, and a very useful one.
Which rights are involved here? Which ones are harmed? Too much, too little, and so on.
Most of you have heard the words right and rights before. But there's some confusion. Which rights are there? Which groups? Are some rights stronger, and some weaker?
Well, lucky you came, because I'm here to put some order into it.
First of all, there's no fixed list that the whole world works by. There are different ways to divide rights. And we'll divide them into three types.
The first type: natural rights. That means rights every person has, simply by being born. You were born, so you have this right.
The right to life and security. You can't just walk down the street and have someone hurt you, kill you, injure you. It's your right not to be harmed.
The right to liberty. To feel, to choose, and to think whatever you want.
Freedom of movement. Freedom of occupation, which means working at whatever you want.
To own property. And the right to equality.
Dignity. And from dignity comes the right to privacy, which is actually the subject of quite a few tasks in the exam.
The second type: civil rights. Once I belong to a certain state, I already have rights in my relationship with that state.
The right to vote and to be elected, freedom of association, freedom of the press, and freedom of expression.
And the third type: social rights. The right to an adequate standard of living. That the state looks after my education, my health, housing, and my employment conditions.

And in history, it went in the same order. First, natural rights were recognised for every person. Then people who felt equal wanted a voice, so, civil rights. And once weaker groups got into government, they created social rights.
Now, if I have money, I don't really need the state to look after my standard of living. I look after myself. Education, health? I go to a private doctor. Housing? I have a villa by the sea.

What's special about social rights is that the state is the one that pays for them. And by the way, they're not guaranteed. Some states don't pay for health, or housing, or workers' rights. It depends on the state you live in.

And some people see social rights as less important than natural rights or civil rights. Why? Well, who pays for social rights? The state. Where does the state get the money? From taxes. And where do taxes come from? From the property of other citizens.
So the very definition of social rights already creates a clash with the right to property. Which is a natural right of every person.
If you get a task with a clash like that, this is a point you might choose to take and develop.
So what about the state? It has a passive role. The state must not harm rights without justification.
Notice, without justification. Because it's completely clear that the state harms our rights, and will keep harming them. It can't be any other way.
Why? Because to protect some rights, it has to harm other rights. For example, I want to drive at a hundred and fifty kilometres an hour, because that's my right. Freedom of movement.
But of course, if I drove that fast, I'd be harming other citizens' right to life and security. So the state harms my right, and doesn't let me drive at that speed. But there's a justification.
Now, who decides if there's a justification? Again, there's no calculator. We need to look at the circumstances of the specific case, and decide.

And sometimes time passes, old decisions come up for discussion again, and the decision changes. Just like an essay. Someone argued for a law, someone argued against, and a law was passed. Thirty years later it's opened again, and suddenly the arguments against are stronger.
The state's second role is an active one. It's not only forbidden to harm rights. It also has to act to protect them.
And like we said, sometimes protecting one right harms another. So with rights arguments, you need to understand that the clash between rights can't be avoided.
It's not like two rights can always live side by side and everything's fine. If that were true, it wouldn't be in our task.
What's important is not to panic about the clash. It's fine that there's a clash. When there is one, we need to make sure the harm to each right is proportionate.
Notice I wrote proportionate harm, not minimal harm. Because it won't always be the minimum. Sometimes I need to harm a right more than the minimum, to protect another right.
So how do we know which right to harm, and what's proportionate? Again, it depends on the circumstances.
Some people will argue that the right to life and security is always bigger than the right to privacy. I mean, if you're dead, what good is your privacy? None.
But that's not what we need to do. We don't talk in general, theoretical terms. We talk about the circumstances of the specific task in front of us.
You want face-recognition cameras, and they harm privacy. In this specific case, the cameras shouldn't be installed. They harm privacy, and their benefit isn't that big.
And then we need to explain why we think the benefit isn't big, and so why the harm isn't proportionate. The harm to privacy is too great.
Now, choosing a rights argument. It's a mixed blessing.

On one hand, no one can deny it. When I make another kind of argument, it's my opinion. I think the cameras will deter people and reduce crime in the filmed area. Okay, that's your opinion. I can already doubt it.
But when I argue that a certain right is harmed, you can't deny the right. It's a fact. Everyone accepts that there's a right, and that it mustn't be harmed, or the harm has to be limited.
But having a right doesn't mean I can say, there's harm to privacy, that's it, I've won the debate. It doesn't work like that.
I need to explain. I need to explain why the harm to the right isn't proportionate, in the specific circumstances of the task.
So on one hand, the start is more solid. I begin with a fact, there is a right. On the other hand, I have to explain, and that's not always easy.
Some students find it easier to just explain the logical chain of an argument that has nothing to do with rights, than to argue and explain why a right is harmed too much, out of proportion.
